summary: This informational RFC describes an EDNS0 option, in active use, that carries information about the network that originated a DNS query and the network the response can be cached for. It has known operational and privacy shortcomings, so a revision was expected.

plainLanguage.summary: A DNS server gets a hint about roughly where you are, so it can send you to a nearby server. That hint reveals some information about you.

questions: what is the ecs option code
how does ecs affect dns caching
does edns client subnet leak my ip address
subtitle: How a DNS resolver can pass part of your network address to a server so it can pick a nearby answer.

tldr.problem: Authoritative servers tailor answers to where the asker is, but they only see the address of the recursive resolver, which may be far from the real user.
tldr.mechanism: An EDNS0 option (code 8) carries a truncated client address and a prefix length to the authoritative server, which answers with a scope saying which networks the answer fits so resolvers can cache it per network.
tldr.outcome: It documents a protocol already in production use, with known operational and privacy shortcomings; the RFC recommends it be off by default and says a revision would follow.

today: RFC 7871 is an Informational RFC, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The abstract says it documents an option in active use and that a revision would be worked through the IETF, but the text does not say whether that happened.

sections.title: Why Resolvers Pass Along the Client Network
sections.content:
Many authoritative nameservers return different answers depending on the perceived topological location of the user. They judge that location from the source IP address of the query. But most queries arrive from recursive resolvers, so the server sees the resolver's address, not the user's.

That works when the resolver is close to its users. It works badly for Centralized Resolvers, which serve query sources that are often not topologically close, including some ISP and organisation setups. This RFC defines an EDNS0 option that conveys enough network information about the originator for the authoritative server to tailor its answer, and lets the server say which range of addresses the answer is meant for.

The option is intended only for resolvers and servers that benefit from it, not for general purpose deployment, and it can safely be ignored by servers that do not implement it.
sections.plainLanguage: A faraway helper only knows where the helper is, not where you are. So the helper is allowed to tell the shop a rough neighbourhood for you.

sections.title: The ECS Option Format
sections.content:
The edns-client-subnet (ECS) option is an EDNS0 option whose OPTION-CODE is 8. After the code and a length come these fields:

  • FAMILY (2 octets): the address family, 1 for IPv4 or 2 for IPv6.
  • SOURCE PREFIX-LENGTH (1 octet): how many leftmost bits of the address are significant. A response mirrors the value from the query.
  • SCOPE PREFIX-LENGTH (1 octet): how many bits of the address the response covers. In queries it MUST be 0.
  • ADDRESS: the address, truncated to SOURCE PREFIX-LENGTH bits and padded with zero bits to the end of the last octet.

A server that receives too few or too many address octets, or non-zero bits beyond the source prefix length, SHOULD return FORMERR. All fields are in network byte order. ECS is defined only for the Internet (IN) DNS class.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a small label stuck on the question. It names the kind of address, how much of it is shown, and later how wide an area the answer is good for.

sections.title: Sending the Option and Building Responses
sections.content:
Recursive resolvers normally add the option when querying authoritative nameservers. If the client query had no ECS option, the resolver sets FAMILY from the client's address and picks a SOURCE PREFIX-LENGTH from its maximum cacheable prefix length, which SHOULD be shorter than the full address for privacy. If the client query had one, the resolver MUST NOT send more bits than the client's source prefix length.

A stub resolver can set a source prefix length to limit what is revealed. A value of 0 means the recursive resolver MUST NOT add the client's address information to its queries.

An authoritative server that implements ECS and receives the option MUST include an ECS option in its response, and the family, source prefix length and address MUST match the query. The SCOPE PREFIX-LENGTH says which network the answer is for. A longer scope than source means the supplied prefix was not specific enough. A shorter scope, possibly 0, means the answer suits a broader range. Servers MUST NOT overlap prefixes. If no ECS option was in the query, none may be in the response.

A server that does not support ECS ought to ignore the option and MUST NOT include one in its replies to signal lack of support.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper tells the shop a blurry neighbourhood. The shop answers and says how big an area its answer is good for, so the helper can reuse it for neighbours.

sections.title: Caching Tailored Answers
sections.content:
Answers tied to a network cannot be handed to everyone, so an ECS-aware resolver stores each Answer-section record with the network from the response. If the scope prefix length is not longer than the source prefix length, the resolver stores the scope-length bits and the answer is valid for that whole range. If the source is shorter than the cache maximum and the scope is longer, the entry is valid only for queries that specify exactly the same source prefix length.

On a cache lookup, the resolver first matches name, type and class, then chooses the entry with the longest prefix match. If no matching network is found it MUST perform resolution as usual, so that tailored answers are not returned to the wrong clients. Records in the Authority and Additional sections MUST NOT be tied to a network. A response with no ECS option is treated as a scope prefix length of 0.

The RFC warns that ECS significantly increases cache size, reduces cache hits and increases server load, though leaving out network-specific caching would likely defeat most of the latency benefit.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper writes each answer on a sticky note labelled with the neighbourhood it fits. Next time someone from that neighbourhood asks, the note is used. Otherwise the helper asks again.

sections.title: Privacy and Security Considerations
sections.content:
With ECS, the network address of the client that started the lookup becomes visible to all servers involved in the resolution, and to any network the DNS packets cross. Section 2 admits that if the mechanism were being designed from scratch it would probably not look like this, and recommends that the feature be turned off by default in all nameserver software.

To limit exposure, recursive resolvers are strongly encouraged to truncate IPv4 addresses to 24 bits and to use 56 bits for IPv6. Users who want their full address hidden can configure their client to send an ECS option with a source prefix length of 0. The RFC notes that support for this opt-out is limited: only one stub resolver, getdns, is known to originate such queries.

Recursive resolvers are also told to send ECS only to authoritative servers known or probed to use it, and never to root, top-level or public-suffix servers.

ECS adds address information to the DNS query tuple, which gives an attacker more room. Spoofed queries with different ECS addresses cause several outgoing queries for the same name, so the attacker has a higher chance of landing a forged response with a scope of 0 that gets cached for all hosts. The defence is that the response's family, address and source prefix length MUST match the query, and resolvers SHOULD discard the whole response if they do not.

Forged ECS data can also pollute caches with results that will rarely be used, help reverse-engineer how an authoritative server picks tailored answers, or push an intermediate server into many extra recursive queries. Mitigations include limiting the networks and answers kept per query and in total, never sending more address bits than the resolver is willing to cache, and treating unroutable addresses as the resolver's own identity.

On DNSSEC, OPT records are not signed. Most DNSSEC records SHOULD be scoped at /0, but RRSIG records MUST be tied to the record set they sign.
sections.plainLanguage: A blurry hint is still a hint about where you live, so blur it or leave it out. Pranksters can also send fake hints, so the helper checks the hint on each answer matches what it sent.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content:
The RFC walks through an IPv6 client whose stub resolver asks a recursive resolver (RNS) for www.example.com. RNS finds nothing cached and, being configured not to send ECS to root and TLD servers, queries them normally. It then queries the authoritative server for example.com with an ECS option: OPTION-CODE 8, FAMILY 2, SOURCE PREFIX-LENGTH 0x38 (56 bits, so the last 72 bits of the address are concealed) and the first 7 octets of the address.

The authoritative server echoes the same family, source prefix length and address, and sets SCOPE PREFIX-LENGTH to 0x30, a /48 network. RNS checks that these match, caches the answer for that network, and replies to the stub resolver without an ECS option because the stub did not send one.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a story of the helper asking the shop with a blurred address, getting an answer marked for a wider neighbourhood, and saving it for later.

fields.name: OPTION-LENGTH
fields.desc: Length of everything after this field, in octets.

fields.name: FAMILY
fields.desc: Address family: 1 for IPv4, 2 for IPv6.

fields.name: SOURCE PREFIX-LENGTH
fields.desc: Leftmost bits of ADDRESS to use. Mirrored in responses.

fields.name: SCOPE PREFIX-LENGTH
fields.desc: Bits the response covers. MUST be 0 in queries.

messages.label: Query www.example.com
messages.note: Asks for recursion; no ECS option.

messages.label: Query + ECS (source /56)
messages.note: Only the first 56 bits of the IPv6 address are sent.

messages.label: Answer + ECS (scope /48)
messages.note: Echoes family, source length and address.

messages.label: Answer, no ECS
messages.note: The stub did not send ECS, so none is returned.
